thread:
olivia: Heads-up — I want to bikeshed the *operator API boundary* for dedicated pool scaling. Is now a good time?
kai: Yep. quick recap: current idea is a tiny operator surface (Reserve/Release/Query) + a separate intent plane that handles headroom.
ben: I still worry the tiny surface hides too much state. operators end up doing guesses and we leak complexity back into the control plane.
sasha: Agree with ben. But large operator APIs are painful for backwards compat and testing. We should pick a stable minimal core and a well-defined extension mechanism.
olivia: That's the tradeoff. Minimal core = easier operator implementations in private deploys. Rich API = more opt-in semantics (soft reservations, priorities, credits).
kai: What if we make core transactional and synchronous but add an async "intent" channel for richer policies? Core handles hard SLO reservations (low latency), intent plane negotiates prewarm/backfill.
ben: Sketch of core API (very small):
```
Reserve(pool, tenant_id, capacity_units) -> {token, granted_units, expiry}
Release(token)
Query(pool, tenant_id) -> {active, headroom_est}
```
The operator only needs to honor tokens atomically. Intent plane decides to issue tokens.
sasha: I like that. It keeps operator trust boundary small. But we need to nail idempotency and lease expiry semantics. If operator crashes, tokens must eventually be reclaimable.
olivia: Good point. We should add a heartbeat TTL and a reclaim path. Also explicit `Revoke(token)` for admin flows.
kai: Also add a `TokenInfo(token)` for debugging, but mark it as read-only and cheap. No heavy semantics.
ben: How do we handle graceful degrade when pool is full? Currently we have fallbacks to smaller-quantized models in hosted mode. For dedicated, tenants expect predictable behavior.
sasha: Proposal: operator enforces soft and hard limits. Tokens can be issued as soft if capacity likely available. Intent plane can upgrade to hard tokens on actual allocation. soft tokens have shorter TTL and lower priority on eviction.
olivia: That introduces two token classes. Complex, but gives us predictable SLOs vs opportunistic capacity. Need to document eviction order clearly.
kai: Observability requirements: per-token lineage (who requested, intent-id, timestamp), allocation events, prewarm indicators. Otherwise debugging will be a nightmare.
ben: Agree. Also add counters for `failed_reserve_reason` (OOS, throttled, pool-drain) so we can triage autoscaler decisions.
sasha: Implementation concerns: operator must be able to reconcile tokens on restart with minimal race windows. We should avoid cross-node locks. Design tokens as lease objects persisted in local k-v store with monotonic sequence for reclaimability.
olivia: Sounds good. Action items:
- kai: draft minimal proto + TTL semantics and `Revoke` semantics (due EOD Friday)
- ben: write a short compatibility note showing how Private deploys can implement with a single-file store or k8s CRD (due Mon)
- sasha: telemetry plan: token metrics + failure reasons (due Wed)
- olivia: append a short section in the operator checklist about eviction order and fallback model mapping (I'll do it)

orch-bot: Deploy-check: no blocking PRs found for the api-draft branch.

ben: One more bikeshed: call them "leases" or "tokens"? I prefer leases (semantic clarity).
kai: "Lease" nails the ttl semantics, but "token" is already used in older notes. I'd rather unify to `lease` in the API and keep `token` as an alias in docs.
olivia: Agreed — `lease` it is. I'll update names in the draft.

sasha: Minor: ensure `Query` can return estimated prewarm latency per tenant so the planner can decide to fall back earlier.
ben: Nice. This is already much clearer than earlier threads. Short RFC next?
olivia: Yes — I'll open an RFC with the proto + upgrade plan + compatibility matrix. Will ping the private-deploy folks for sign-off.
kai: ping me when RFC lands, I'll sanity-check the operator-level race diagrams.
ben: Thanks all. Closing the bikeshed for now :thumbsup:
